newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan fighters agree to hand key pass to Taleban.
newsitem.headline: Afghan fighters agree to hand key pass to Taleban.

text.p: The Islamic Taleban militia on Sunday were poised to take control of the Salang Pass, Afghanistan's strategic north-south gateway, after an enemy commander defending it declared he had joined them.

"The people of Salang have made an uprising against the forces of evil and corruption, and I call on all the people of Salang to rise against the communists. I am a Talib," opposition commander Basir Salangi told a crowd of Taleban fighters shouting "Allah-u-Akbar (God is greatest)".
Salangi had just come to an agreement with a council of Taleban commanders in the town of Jebel-us-Seraj, at the the foot of the Salang Pass.

He called his fighters on a walkie-talkie to tell them of the agreement. Thousands of Taleban fighters, loaded on tanks, trucks and four-wheel drive jeeps cheered Salangi as he was driven up towards the front line.
They anticipated an easy advance through the 11,000-foot (3,350 m) pass to the northern limits of Salangi's command, the village of Khinjan.

But artillery shells fell close to the waiting Taleban convoy as equipment was brought up to repair a bridge that the opposition had blown up to block just such an advance. There were no immediate reports of casualties.

A Taleban commander at the pass estimated that the bridge would be installed by midnight (1930 GMT). The deal to hand over the Salang came a day after forces allied to the Taleban took Mazar-i-Sharif in the north of Afghanistan, the opposition's capital.

Remaining opposition forces are being squeezed by Taleban forces moving south from Mazar-i-Sharif and north from Kabul. Ahmed Shah Masood, the chief military commander of the government ousted from Kabul by the Taleban last September, is holding out in the Panjsher valley close to the Salang Pass.

Taleban fighters said they believed that Masood's forces were responsible for the shelling of the convoy. If the Salang falls, as the Taleban expect, it will cut the last link between Masood and Hezb-i-Wahadat, a mainly Shi'ite faction still fighting to retain control of central Afghanistan's Bamiyan province.

The fall of Mazar-i-Sharif, the opposition's main point of supply as well as their political capital, dealt a severe blow to the opposition. They now control less than 10 per cent of the country and are confined to mountainous territory in the northeast and centre of Afghanistan.
